extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, society and commercial publishers, editorial staff, and publishing consultants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for publishers/editors considering launching or operating a cascade (transfer) journal built from manuscripts rejected by an upstream title, focusing on manuscript flow, quality, reputation, indexing, and financial viability. Uses a numeric example to illustrate conversion rates and risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript flow sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: If current submissions cannot support a new journal, then it should reconsider the prospect before devoting itself (its staff and its money) to a new title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article uses a hypothetical ASIE J example (1000 submissions, 40% peer-reviewed, 10% overall acceptance) to show that apparent upstream volume can be misleading: after accounting for desk-rejects, transfers, editor acceptance rates, and author acceptance of transfer, a new journal might end up with very few publishable papers (example resulted in just 50 published papers). Initial manuscript flow must be much greater; the new journal needs to attract its own submissions or rely on other strategies (commissioning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer mechanisms and preservation of reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Today, transfer is often built into the submission process of many journals. When manuscripts transfer, reviews and editorial decisions can go with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical capability of submission systems matters (authors may select secondary/tertiary titles during upload); transfer-with-reviews reduces resubmission friction but does not solve underlying flow/quality problems. Publishers should confirm systems and policies support seamless transfer and appropriate sharing of reviewer comments and decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid diluting exclusivity/brand
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers (and editorial boards) may support publishing more papers in theory, only they want these papers to go somewhere else, lest they dilute the exclusivity of the journal and its brand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors are hesitant to be associated with a “journal of rejects.” Creating lower-tier sibling journals risks reputational damage to the family of titles; publishers must weigh growth against brand dilution and perceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception: 'journal of rejects' and confidentiality vs transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping rejection and transfer information private and confidential provides a poignant counter-argument to calls for transparency in peer review and publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are excellent arguments for increasing transparency, but publishers and editors may prefer confidentiality to avoid stigmatizing transferred manuscripts or secondary journals. Consider reputational effects of public transfer histories and how transparency policies will be implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain parent journal selectivity and standing
rubrics_metrics.description: ASIE J cannot afford to be less picky or risk its standing among its competitors. If ASIE J is too picky, it risks angering its society membership and author base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce the primary title’s standards simply to feed a cascade; maintain the parent journal’s selectivity and reputation. Balance between protecting standing and supporting a cascade must be carefully managed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author acceptance/conversion of transfer offers
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may decline offers to publish in a new journal — e.g., in the hypothetical, only one-half of corresponding authors accepted the editor’s offer to publish in ASIE-Two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversion rate from transfer offer to accepted publication is a critical metric; low author acceptance reduces the effective yield of a cascade. Track and model likely conversion rates when forecasting output for a new journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing and performance ratings require sufficient volume/quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Until ASIE-Two can start attracting its own submission flow, it will need to rely on its parent journal for support. However, ASIE-Two cannot afford to remain unindexed and not receive any recognized performance ratings — this will make it difficult to attract its own submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A new journal’s inability to be indexed or receive recognized metrics (impact factor, etc.) hampers recruitment of authors. Plan for strategies (commissioning, editorial board recruitment, quality assurance) to reach indexing thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplement cascaded content with commissioning and leadership buy-in
rubrics_metrics.description: One would need to supplement those [cascaded] articles with a strong commissioning program, particularly calling in leaders of the society to supplement the growth of their own group’s journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying solely on rejected manuscripts is insufficient. Proactive commissioning, invited submissions, and recruiting respected authors can seed a journal, improve indexing chances, and provide independent submission flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term financial viability timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Think about the establishment of a new journal as a long-term project. Rule of thumb (subscription era): successful journal runs in the black within 5 to 7 years and pays off costs in 7 to 10 years; open access dynamics differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should plan for multi-year investment horizons. Open access might enable earlier revenue, but expect a long-term commitment before profitability and sustainable submission/reader bases are achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid publishing mediocre or poorly executed science
rubrics_metrics.description: If a given paper does not meet the highest applicable standard for publication in its field, it should not be published. We should avoid the cascade approach altogether and hold each paper to the highest standards applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cascading must not become a mechanism to publish weak work. Editors and publishers should resist creating journals whose purpose is to absorb substandard papers; uphold scientific rigor and data quality across all titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility to identify and communicate fatal flaws
rubrics_metrics.description: It is incumbent on the editors or reviewers to convey the fatal flaws to the authors so that those studies don’t just cascade (wasting everyone’s time in the process) into the Journal of Poorly Executed [Discipline of Choice].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review should clearly identify fatal methodological or reporting flaws; strong editorial feedback can prevent wasteful cascades of flawed studies. Good review practices reduce downstream burden on secondary journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependency risk for the secondary journal and reputational danger of being a 'dumping ground'
rubrics_metrics.description: If that secondary journal becomes reliant on the cast off from the primary journal and authorship is looked upon as being less than sterling then authors will not agree to being in the secondary journal. Worst still the secondary journal may lose all its authorship because it becomes known as a dumping ground!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary journals should aim to build independent identity, standards, and submission pipelines; avoid dependence on transfers as the sole source of content to prevent long-term reputational decline and author attrition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cascading can be topical and maintain standards (nuanced use)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are 'cascading' practices that are a lot more nuanced than quality. Papers move between journals for topical fit — e.g., a broad Structural Engineering journal may transfer construction-related papers to specialist construction journals while applying the same level of peer review under the same standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cascades used for better topical placement (not to relax standards) can be legitimate and beneficial. Ensure transferred manuscripts receive equivalent peer review standards in the receiving title and that subject fit—not lower bar—is the reason for transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use data and tracking tools to understand rejected-manuscript fate
rubrics_metrics.description: Data tracking the fate of rejected manuscripts can be found in products such as HighWire’s Rejected-Article Tracker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should analyze empirical data on submission, transfer, acceptance, and downstream publication outcomes to make informed decisions about launching cascades and forecasting realistic yields and impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market and mission balance — business realities versus editorial mission
rubrics_metrics.description: One has to balance mission and business; in a competitive world which demands top and bottom line performance it seems that quality is suffering. Journals that can’t at least support their own costs after a period of initial investment won’t survive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider financial pressures, author incentives (e.g., APCs or institutional requirements), and mission-driven goals when evaluating cascade strategies. Be mindful that market competition can push publishers toward practices that may compromise editorial standards; plan safeguards.
